procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a lower court where the respondents were initially tried and acquitted under s. 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated June 26, 1968, of the Kerala High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 113 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Kerala High Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 113 of 1968 and confirmed the acquittal of the respondents.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Food Inspector, Calicut Corporation, appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and order of the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sale of an adulterated article of food to a Food Inspector for analysis constitutes an offense under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, even if the seller does not offer that article for sale as a standalone product but only uses it as an ingredient in other preparations.

facts: A Food Inspector purchased sugar from the respondents' tea stall for the purpose of analysis.
The sugar was subsequently found to be adulterated.
The respondents argued that they were not guilty of an offense because they did not sell sugar as a standalone product, but only kept it to use as an ingredient in the tea they sold to customers.
law: Section 2(xiii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, provides a special definition of "sale" that explicitly includes a sale of an article of food for analysis.
Section 7 of the Act prohibits any person from selling an adulterated article of food.
Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Act makes it a punishable offense for any person to sell adulterated food.
application: The Court established that the transaction between the Food Inspector and the tea stall owner was a "sale" within the specific meaning of Section 2(xiii) of the Act, because it was a sale for analysis.
Once the transaction was legally defined as a "sale," all the consequences of a sale under the Act applied.

The Court held that it is irrelevant whether the article was intended for sale as a standalone product or whether the seller was a regular dealer in that specific article. The text states, "it is of no consequence that the said article was not intended to be sold as such by the accused."
Because the sugar was an adulterated article of food and it was legally "sold" to the Food Inspector, the respondents had committed an offense under Sections 7 and 16(1)(a)(i) of the Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the sale of an adulterated article of food to a Food Inspector for analysis constitutes a punishable offense under the Act. This is because the Act's definition of "sale" specifically includes a sale for analysis, making it irrelevant whether the seller intended to sell the item as a standalone product or was a dealer in that particular food article.

issue.issue_text: Whether sugar, kept for the purpose of being mixed into tea for sale, qualifies as an 'article of food' under Section 2(5) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.

facts: The accused ran a tea stall and kept sugar on the premises.
This sugar was not for sale by itself, but was intended to be mixed into tea, which was then sold to customers.
A Food Inspector purchased a sample of this sugar, which was later found to be adulterated.
law: Under Section 2(5) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, an 'article of food' includes any article which ordinarily enters into or is used in the composition or preparation of human food.
application: The Supreme Court found that there was no real dispute that sugar is an article used for human consumption.
The Court highlighted that even the tea stall owners (the respondents) admitted that the sugar was kept for the purpose of being used in the preparation of tea sold to customers.
This intended use squarely fits the legal definition of an 'article of food' because it is an article "used in the composition or preparation of human food."
Therefore, whether the sugar was sold 'as such' or was merely an ingredient for another product was irrelevant to its classification as an 'article of food' under the Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that sugar kept for the purpose of being mixed into tea for sale qualifies as an 'article of food' under Section 2(5) of the Act, because the definition includes any article used in the composition or preparation of human food.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sale of an adulterated article of food to a Food Inspector for analysis constitutes an offense under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, even if the seller does not offer that article for sale as a standalone product but only uses it as an ingredient in other preparations.
appellant_arguments: The view of the lower courts that the respondents are not guilty because they are not 'dealers in sugar as such' is erroneous.
Once an article of food is sold to a Food Inspector and is found to be adulterated, an offense is committed under the Act.
The fact that the seller is not a dealer in that specific item or that the item is only used as an ingredient is irrelevant to the commission of the offense.
respondent_arguments: To be held liable, it must be established that the respondents were 'dealers in sugar as such'.
The acquittal is justified because the sugar was not for sale as a standalone product but was only intended to be used as an ingredient in the preparation of tea.

arguments.issue_text: Whether sugar, kept for the purpose of being mixed into tea for sale, qualifies as an 'article of food' under Section 2(5) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's entire case presupposes that sugar is an 'article of food' under the Act. By arguing that its sale, when adulterated, constitutes an offense, they implicitly affirm that its status as an ingredient for tea does not remove it from the Act's definition or purview.
respondent_arguments: The respondents did not argue that sugar is not an 'article of food'. Instead, they argued that because it was kept only for the purpose of being mixed with tea and not for sale as sugar itself, they should not be held liable for an offense.

statutes.section: Rule 5 and Appendix B, item A. 07.01

cases.case_name: Municipal Board, Faizabad v. Lal Chand Surajmal and another
cases.principle: When there is a sale of an adulterated article of food to a Food Inspector, the accused is guilty of an offence under s. 16(1)(a)(i) read with s. 7 of the Act, and it is not necessary that the person selling the article be a dealer in that article as such, nor that the article was taken from a larger quantity intended for sale.

cases.case_name: The Public Prosecutor v. Palanisami Nadar
cases.principle: When there is a sale of an adulterated article of food to a Food Inspector, the accused is guilty of an offence under s. 16(1)(a)(i) read with s. 7 of the Act, and it is not necessary that the person selling the article be a dealer in that article as such, nor that the article was taken from a larger quantity intended for sale.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A sale of an article of food to a Food Inspector for the purpose of analysis constitutes a 'sale' under the Act. If the article sold is found to be adulterated, the seller commits an offense, and it is not necessary for the prosecution to establish that the seller is a dealer in that specific article.
obiter: The appellant has argued the appeal only as a test case and does not challenge the acquittal of the respondents.
Apart from holding the respondents technically guilty, the court is not setting aside the order of acquittal passed in their favour.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: On the finding of the two courts the sugar in question has been found to be adulterated. The purchase by the Food Inspector from the accused of sugar for purposes of analysis is a sale under s. 2(13) of the Act. Section 7 prohibits a person from selling adulterated article of food. Similarly, under s. 16(1)(a)(i) any person who sells adulterated food commits an offence and is punishable therein. The sugar which is the commodity before us is food under s. 2(5) of the Act. In this case the sale was for analysis and the article was an article of food and in view of the concurrent findings of both the courts that it was adulterated, the respondents have contravened ss. 7 and I 6(l)(a)(i) of the Act. Hence it must be held that the respondents are technically guilty of the offence with which they were charged.
legal_tests_applied: Whether an article qualifies as 'food' under Section 2(5) of the Act, which includes any article which ordinarily enters into or is used in the composition or preparation of human food.
Whether a transaction constitutes a 'sale' under Section 2(13) of the Act, which includes a sale of any article of food for analysis.
Whether the act of selling an adulterated food item constitutes an offense under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Act, which applies to 'any person who sells' such an item.
Whether the Act requires a person to be a 'dealer' in a specific article of food to be held liable for its sale when adulterated.
